title: Agent-sandbox isolation becomes a named procurement requirement by H1 2027
body: The Claude Cowork sandbox-escape chain that Armadin disclosed and Anthropic patched on June 30 is the kind of failure mode that turns a vendor's private security posture into a buyer-side line item. The escape did not exploit a novel memory bug; it abused a resume flag that skipped unprivileged-user creation and a domain-override parameter that disabled the network allowlist, meaning the containment boundary itself was the attack surface. That an agent-security startup, Straiker, closed a $64M Series A in the same week for exactly this class of runtime guardrail confirms a defensive market is capitalizing around the agent runtime rather than around the model. The prediction is that enterprise buyers of agentic tools will begin demanding explicit, testable evidence of runtime isolation, namespace hardening, seccomp posture, capability minimization, and network-egress default-deny, as a documented procurement requirement rather than a trust-us assurance. The forcing function is governance-adjacent: with the UN's Geneva dialogue and its new scientific panel putting agent cyber-misuse on the rulemaking agenda this week, the vendor-versus-researcher dispute over whether a sandbox escape even counts as a security issue is precisely the ambiguity that procurement language and eventual disclosure norms resolve. Expect agentic-tool RFPs and enterprise security questionnaires to carry a dedicated agent-sandbox-isolation section, with third-party red-team attestation increasingly attached, before the first half of 2027 closes.
